name: Verb Phrase

dimensions.form: Phrase headed by a verb, with complements and modifiers licensed in the VP; no Subject occurs within the VP
dimensions.meaning: A situation profile contributed by the head verb and elaborated by its internal dependents
dimensions.function: Head (Predicate) of a Clause, or dependent in constructions that license a VP
dimensions.distribution: Occurs as the Head of a Clause and in selected embedded or modifying environments

1.definition: A phrase headed by a verb, containing any complements and modifiers but excluding the Subject
1.details: The verb is the Head of the VP and the ultimate Head of any Clause headed by that VP. Its lexical sense and constructional frame jointly determine which complements are required or permitted. The Subject, when present, is a dependent of Clause rather than VP; a VP can therefore serve as the Head of a Clause with an overt Subject or as the whole overt content of a subjectless Clause.

examples.note: Head V left with modifier early; Kim is Subject of Clause, not part of the VP
Head V sent with indirect and direct object complements
Head V slept with a construction-licensed object and PP complement

constraints.description: The Head is a verb; its inflectional form and lexical sense constrain the VP's internal syntax.
Complements and VP-level modifiers are dependents within the VP.
A Subject is never a dependent within VP structure; it belongs to the Clause headed by the VP.

projection.target: Once a constituent is identified as a VP, the head verb and its constructional frame predict the inventory and order of internal complements, while the constituent type is eligible to serve as the Head of both subject-bearing and subjectless Clauses
projection.evidence: CGEL states that the verb is Head of VP and that properties of the verb determine which other elements are required or permitted; the Clause/VP contrast independently locates Subject outside the VP

grounds.note: The verbal head and its sense license complement inventory, while VP category predicts Clause-head distribution
Verb as Head of VP and ultimate Head of Clause; verb properties govern permitted and required dependents

diagnostics: Subject combines with VP at Clause level
manner, temporal, aspectual, and other integrated modifiers

relatedConstructions.notes: VP specializes the headed Phrase pattern with V as Head

grounds.note: VP is a phrasal category headed by V and serves as the Predicate/Head of Clause

curious.title: The verb and what goes with it
curious.summary: A verb phrase is a verb together with the words that complete or modify it, not including the subject.
curious.body: In Kim left early, the verb is left and early adds to it. Together, left early is the verb phrase. Kim, who did the leaving, stands outside it. A verb phrase can be bigger. In I sent Sue a copy, the verb sent comes with two objects, Sue and a copy. In They slept the afternoon away, the verb comes with an object and another word that finishes it. The verb's meaning and the pattern it appears in together decide which other words are required or allowed, and the subject is never inside the verb phrase. The dictionary marks this account as provisional.
curious.try: Take Kim left early and cover up the subject, Kim. What's left, left early, is the verb phrase.

teacher.summary: Core grammar category: the verb phrase, with its head verb and dependents, excluding the Subject.
teacher.explain: A verb phrase (VP) is a phrase headed by a verb, containing any complements and modifiers but excluding the Subject. The verb is the head of the VP and the ultimate head of any clause headed by that VP. Its lexical sense and constructional frame jointly determine which complements are required or permitted. The Subject is a dependent of the clause, not of the VP. A VP can therefore head a clause with an overt Subject, or be the whole overt content of a subjectless clause. This dictionary marks its analysis provisional.
teacher.terms: Verb phrase is the standard term. In this grammar the VP excludes the Subject, and Predicate names the VP's function in the clause.

contrasts.note: Kim is the Subject of the clause, not part of the VP.

watch_for: A learner might include the Subject in the verb phrase, when the Subject belongs to the clause.
A learner might assume a verb takes any complements, though its sense and frame decide which are required or permitted.
teacher.activity: Students take simple sentences with a clear subject and bracket the verb phrase, leaving out the subject. They then compare brackets in pairs.

checked.note: Fixed: curious.body now says the verb's sense and the constructional frame jointly decide which complements are required or permitted, as in the entry (not the verb alone); curious.try no longer tells readers to cross out the subject of any sentence they say (other material, such as a vocative, can lie outside the VP) and uses Kim left early; teacher activity limited to simple sentences with a clear subject; replaced 'the entry' with 'this dictionary'.
